answer: node2vec does not rely on a pure DFS traversal strategy. Instead, it uses biased random walks with two parameters, p and q, to interpolate between BFS-like and DFS-like exploration. A low q biases walks to move outward from the current node, which can make the sampled neighborhoods more DFS-like, while a high q biases walks to stay close, which is more BFS-like. The embeddings are then learned from these walks using a skip-gram objective, so node2vec can capture structural equivalence or homophily depending on the walk bias, but it is not restricted to DFS-style equivalence only.
